paragraphs.text: We owe future generations at least a world that is no worse than the one we were given. People who are not born yet cannot vote or complain, but that does not make their interests count for less. If anything, they are more vulnerable, because they depend entirely on choices made before they arrive. Their claim on us is like the claim of a stranger in another country: real, even if we never meet them. Derek Parfit and Samuel Scheffler both defend some version of this view, for different reasons.

paragraphs.text: Think about a city that builds a dam it knows will fail in eighty years. Nobody alive today will be hurt when it fails, but we would still say the builders did something wrong. Engineers who cut corners on purpose would not be excused because their victims were born later, and we would blame them even more if they had simply saved money. The harm is real even though the people harmed do not exist yet. This shows that time alone does not cancel a duty.

paragraphs.text: Parfit's non-identity problem is the strongest objection. Our choices change which people are born, so the people of the future cannot complain that we made them worse off. Without our choices they would not exist at all. Parfit himself thought the problem was real and spent years looking for a principle that avoids it. If no particular person is made worse off, it can seem that no one is wronged. The objection shows that 'harm' is the wrong word, not that we owe nothing: we can owe future people a decent world without making any particular person better off.

paragraphs.text: Climate policy is the clearest case. Every ton of carbon we burn now makes storms and droughts worse for people a century from now. Sea walls, crop failures and heat waves will fall hardest on people who had no say in our choices. Cutting emissions costs us something today, but a few percent of income now weighs little against homes and harvests lost for generations. Even a small chance of these harms should count, because so many people will live through them.

paragraphs.from_text: We owe future generations at least a world that is no worse than the one we were given. People who are not born yet cannot vote or complain, but that does not make their interests count for less. If anything, they are more vulnerable, because they depend entirely on choices made before they arrive. Their claim on us is like the claim of a stranger in another country: real, even if we never meet them. Most philosophers now accept some version of this view.
paragraphs.to_text: We owe future generations at least a world that is no worse than the one we were given. People who are not born yet cannot vote or complain, but that does not make their interests count for less. If anything, they are more vulnerable, because they depend entirely on choices made before they arrive. Their claim on us is like the claim of a stranger in another country: real, even if we never meet them. Derek Parfit and Samuel Scheffler both defend some version of this view, for different reasons.

paragraphs.from_text: Think about a city that builds a dam it knows will fail in eighty years. Nobody alive today will be hurt when it fails, but we would still say the builders did something wrong. Engineers who cut corners on purpose would not be excused because their victims were born later, and we would blame them even more if they had simply saved money. The harm is real even though the people harmed do not exist yet, this shows that time alone does not cancel a duty.
paragraphs.to_text: Think about a city that builds a dam it knows will fail in eighty years. Nobody alive today will be hurt when it fails, but we would still say the builders did something wrong. Engineers who cut corners on purpose would not be excused because their victims were born later, and we would blame them even more if they had simply saved money. The harm is real even though the people harmed do not exist yet. This shows that time alone does not cancel a duty.

paragraphs.from_text: Parfit's non-identity problem is the strongest objection. Our choices change which people are born, so the people of the future cannot complain that we made them worse off, without our choices they would not exist at all. Parfit himself thought the problem was real and spent years looking for a principle that avoids it. If no particular person is made worse off, it can seem that no one is wronged. I think this objection is clever but it does not change what we should do.
paragraphs.to_text: Parfit's non-identity problem is the strongest objection. Our choices change which people are born, so the people of the future cannot complain that we made them worse off. Without our choices they would not exist at all. Parfit himself thought the problem was real and spent years looking for a principle that avoids it. If no particular person is made worse off, it can seem that no one is wronged. The objection shows that 'harm' is the wrong word, not that we owe nothing: we can owe future people a decent world without making any particular person better off.

paragraphs.from_text: Climate policy is the clearest case. Every ton of carbon we burn now makes storms and droughts worse for people a century from now. Sea walls, crop failures and heat waves will fall hardest on people who had no say in our choices. Cutting emissions costs us something today, but the cost to them is much larger. Even a small chance of these harms should count, because so many people will live through them.

paragraphs.from_text: So we do owe something to future generations. What we owe is not everything we have, but at least a world no worse than ours (Parfit 1984). That is a modest duty, and it is one we are failing. Recycling and voting are not enough; the duty asks for real limits on what we take.
